newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S. Korea looks for evidence of kickbacks by Hanbo.
newsitem.headline: S. Korea looks for evidence of kickbacks by Hanbo.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors Sunday searched for evidence of kickbacks by the troubled Hanbo Group with President Kim Young-sam calling huge loans to the conglomerate a typical example of corruption.
State prosecutors said they were questioning officials of Hanbo and creditor banks over a lobbying fund kept by Hanbo founder Chung Tae-soo who was arrested on Friday.
"An investigation is under way over how and how much the fund was raised," one prosecution official said. "The prosecutors are also examining Hanbo's bank accounts to trace irregularities."
Chung was arrested a few days after Kim ordered a thorough probe into billions of dollars of loans funnelled to Hanbo Steel Co. that was declared insolvent on Jan. 23.
Hanbo Steel, flagship of South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate, had piled up five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans to build a new mill in Tangjin on the southwestern coast.
At a weekend meeting with his top aides at the presidential Blue House, Kim deplored the loan scandal and expressed frustration over his anti-graft campaign.
"I believe the Hanbo case is a typical example of irregularities and corruption," Kim's spokesman quoted the president as saying.
"Unless corruption is eradicated, the future of our country will be dismal," Kim was quoted as saying.
Both ruling and opposition parties have accused rival members of parliament of peddling influence to press banks into offering loans exceeding the value of collateral.
The opposition has also accused Kim's close associates of involvement in the loan scandal. Prosecutors said they would investigate all allegations relating to the loans.

The Hanbo scandal has embarrassed Kim, who has striven for a reputation as an anti-corruption crusader. Kim's popularity, which topped 90 percent when he launched an anti-graft drive shortly after he took office in 1993, now approaches single digits according to some recent surveys.

With presidential elections about 10 months away, the ruling camp is also smarting from a humiliating retreat over a new labour law it was forced to send back to parliament after nearly a month of industrial strife.

Political parties have agreed to launch a separate parliamentary probe into Hanbo and discuss the controversial labour law but wrangling over procedures have prevented them from setting a date to reconvene the National Assembly.
Analysts said a protracted debate over the law, which makes it easier for companies to fire workers and replace strikers, would damage his New Korea Party in the elections in December.
Kim is barred by the constitution from seeking a second term but he is believed to be trying to extend his influence by installing a protege in office.

The main opposition National Congress for New Politics said the Hanbo scandal highlighted a continuing corrupt alliance between politics and business which Kim called a legacy of the military-backed rule of his predecessors.

Chung paid 15 billion won ($17.4 million) into a slush fund raised by former president Roh Tae-woo, now serving a 17-year jail term for corruption and human rights abuses. But a Seoul court trying Chung and Roh acquitted Chung on the grounds the money was forcibly extracted.
He was also convicted of bribery in a multi-million dollar housing scandal involving Hanbo Group's construction unit in 1991.
